We are part of the Department of Biochemistry & Molecular Biophysics at the University of California, San Diego. ​We are committed to fostering an inclusive and collaborative environment, where curiosity and innovation thrive. Whether you're a fellow researcher, student, or simply curious about science, we invite you to explore our work and join us in celebrating the wonders of molecular biology! Regulation of gene expression We are interested in how gene expression is regulated in human mitochondria and bacteria. We explore how RNA polymerase, the central enzyme in gene expression, regulates transcription through pausing, coordinates RNA synthesis with DNA replication and RNA processing in mitochondria, and how these processes can be harnessed to manipulate gene expression for developing antimicrobials and treating diseases. learn more Exciting news! June 2026 Dr. Tatiana Mishanina has been promoted to Associate Professor! Thanks for all you do for us and congratulations!! July 2026 Congratulations to Dr. Danea Palmer for a perfect thesis defense! We are all so proud of you and know you're going to do great things!! September 2026 Danea and Avery's paper is officially accepted to Nucleic Acids Research ! Congratulations you two and great work! Read it here ! sources.text: THE MISHANINA LAB Home Research Publications Team Lab Life Join Triton TRaCK Outreach Announcements Links Our Projects Co-transcriptional folding of RNA in bacteria Riboswitches are 5'-untranslated regions of mRNA that control the fate of their respective transcript, typically in response to ligand binding. We are studying an unusual, “pH-responsive element” (PRE) riboswitch at the alx gene locus in E. coli , which encodes a putative transition metal ion transporter. PRE folding is in part kinetically controlled: RNA polymerase (RNAP) pausing promotes folding of the PRE into one of the two possible structures to allow or inhibit ribosome binding to mRNA and translation of the downstream gene. We found that RNAP pausing is not the whole story, however. The RNA itself appears to "sense" changes in pH and rearrange its structure accordingly. We are currently investigating the details of this process using chemical probing of RNA structure (SHAPE-MaP), single-particle cryo-EM of transcription complexes, and in vitro transcription assays. Ultimately, we want to piece together the folding pathway of the RNA at different pH. The findings from this project will drive design of pH-responsive sensors for microbial engineering, which has diagnostic and therapeutic applications. Transcription in human mitochondria and processes coupled to it ​ Human mitochondrial genome (h-mtDNA, ~16 kb circle) encodes peptides of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes and RNAs needed for their translation within the mitochondria. Transcription of h-mtDNA, carried out by a structurally distinct RNAP (POLRMT), lies at the heart of mitochondrial gene expression. We are interested in the mechanism and biological roles of POLRMT pausing during transcription. For example, do pauses provide a time window for RNAs to be chemically modified and/or excised out of the long, polycistronic transcript? Do the pauses play a role in the switch from transcription to h-mtDNA replication? ​We are also interested in the curious dual function of the mitochondria transcription factor A (TFAM), which on the one hand helps POLRMT start transcription on h-mtDNA, while on the other hand serves as the main h-mtDNA packaging protein. We showed that by post-translationally modifying TFAM, it is possible to preserve these two important functions while making TFAM a weaker barrier to a transcribing POLRMT. We are grateful to UCSD, UCSD Cryo-EM Facility, Burroughs Welcome Fund, NIH R35, NIH Molecular Biophysics and Interfaces Training Grants, and Yinan Wang Memorial Junior Faculty Fellowship for research support .
